subject: biology

items.q: Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make a particular antibody. They are then combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. What does the tumour cell allow the hybridoma cell to do?
items.correct: Divide to produce many identical cells.
items.misconception: Make the antibody that is later collected.
items.why: Students associate tumour cells with rapid growth and treat them as the active partner, and the word hybridoma sounds like a kind of tumour. The role of the lymphocyte is easily lost because the stimulation step happens before the two cells are combined. Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make a particular antibody, and these lymphocytes are combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. It is the hybridoma cell formed that can both divide and make the antibody.
items.random_wrong: Make a different antibody as it divides.

items.q: A monoclonal antibody is collected from a clone of hybridoma cells and used to measure the level of one hormone in blood. Why does it bind only to that hormone?
items.correct: It is specific to one binding site on one antigen.
items.misconception: It is made by a mixture of many different cells.
items.why: Collecting and purifying a large amount of antibody sounds like bulk production from many sources, and students often read monoclonal as meaning many clones rather than one clone. Monoclonal antibodies are produced from a single clone of cells. Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody, and a large amount of that antibody can be collected and purified.
items.random_wrong: It is made by one particular kind of tumour cell.

items.q: A patient with cancer is given a monoclonal antibody that has been bound to a toxic drug. The antibody binds to an antigen found on the patient's cancer cells. How does this treatment work?
items.correct: It delivers the toxic drug to the cancer cells.
items.misconception: It carries the toxic drug to every body cell.
items.why: Earlier work on the immune response describes antibodies in general terms as attacking pathogens, so students carry over a picture of antibodies as general purpose defence molecules rather than as molecules with one binding site. Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen and so are able to target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.
items.random_wrong: It stops the toxic drug causing side effects.

items.q: Which statement about monoclonal antibodies is correct?
items.correct: They create more side effects than expected.
items.misconception: They bind to several different protein antigens.
items.why: Earlier work on the immune response describes antibodies in general terms as attacking pathogens, so students carry over a picture of antibodies as general purpose defence molecules rather than as molecules with one binding site. Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen and so are able to target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.
items.random_wrong: They create fewer side effects than expected.

items.q: Why are monoclonal antibodies not yet as widely used as everyone hoped when they were first developed?
items.correct: Because they create more side effects than expected.
items.misconception: Monoclonal antibodies cause no side effects, because they only bind to the cells they are meant to target.
items.why: The statement that the antibody delivers a substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body is generalised into the idea that the treatment cannot harm the patient at all. Monoclonal antibodies create more side effects than expected. They are not yet as widely used as everyone hoped when they were first developed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a monoclonal antibody bound to a toxic drug treat cancer?
items.correct: It delivers the toxic drug to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.
items.misconception: The monoclonal antibody itself destroys the cancer cell that it binds to, so the substance bound to it is not needed.
items.why: Students carry over from the immune response the idea that antibodies deal with the cells they attach to, so they see binding itself as the killing step rather than as a way of delivering something. For cancer, the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical which stops cells growing and dividing. It delivers the substance to the cancer cells.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
